meta.title: Latin A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Latin → English (see the Latin, recall the meaning) and English → Latin (see an English meaning, recall the Latin). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no examination publishes a graded Latin word list, and the Common European Framework of Reference describes living languages, so this deck borrows the framework's A1 band only as a SCOPE — the everyday topics whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — and is Folio's own list, not any examination's. 322 of the 500 words come from a vocabulary written for that scope, in the words of Roman life: greetings and politeness, people and the family, numbers, time, food and drink, buying and selling, the house, the town and travel, the body and illness, the sky and the weather, colours, animals, the commonest describing words and verbs, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of. The other 178 are the commonest remaining words of classical Latin, by their rank in the Dickinson College Commentaries Latin Core Vocabulary, and the cards are dealt by that rank, so the words a reader of Latin meets most often come first; the few the list does not hold follow, ordered by how often they appear in the Tatoeba corpus. Every headword is printed with its macrons, the marks over a long vowel (amō, rēgīna), and with its dictionary entry beneath it: a verb's principal parts (amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum), a noun's genitive and gender (rēx, rēgis m.), an adjective's three genders (bonus, bona, bonum). The 212 nouns and 102 verbs, and the adjectives and pronouns, carry their whole table behind the All forms fold — every case in both numbers; a verb's five indicative tenses, present subjunctive, imperative, infinitives and participles. Example sentences come with 499 of the 500 words, three apiece for 499 of them, with the word picked out in colour. The speaker reads Latin with an Italian voice, which gives the Italianate church pronunciation rather than the classical one, because almost no device has a Latin voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale, as a scope only. Frequency: the Dickinson College Commentaries Latin Core Vocabulary (Christopher Francese and others, 2012–13), CC BY-SA 3.0. Meanings, gender, principal parts, macrons and tables: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

"Nate, quis indomitas tantus dolor excitat iras? / Quid furis, aut quonam nostri tibi cura recessit?"

"Et jam nox humida cœlo / præcipitat suadentque cadentia sidera somnos. / Sed si tantus amor casus cognoscere nostros / et breviter Trojæ supremum audire laborem, / quamquam animus meminisse horret luctuque refugit, / incipiam."
"And now already from the heaven's high steep / the dewy night wheels down, and sinking slow, / the stars are gently wooing us to sleep. / But, if thy longing be so great to know / the tale of Troy's last agony and woe, / the toils we suffered, though my heart doth ache, / and grief would fain the memory forego / of scenes so sad, yet, Lady, for thy sake / I will begin," and thus the sire of Troy outspake:

I reach the ramparts and the shadowy gates / whence first I issued, backward through the night / my studied steps retracing. Horror waits / around; the very silence breeds affright.
"Jam jam nulla mora est; sequor et, qua ducitis, adsum. / Di patrii, servate domum, servate nepotem! / Vestrum hoc augurium,vestroque in numine Troja est. / Cedo equidem nec, nate, tibi comes ire recuso."
"Now, now," he cries, "no tarrying; wheresoe'er / ye point the path, I follow and am there. / Gods of my fathers! O preserve to-day / my home, preserve my grandchild; for your care / is Troy, and yours this omen. I obey; / lead on, my son, I yield and follow on thy way."
Hic mihi nescio quod trepido male numen amicum / confusam eripuit mentem: namque avia cursu / dum sequor et nota excedo regione viarum, / heu, misero conjux fatone erepta Creusa / subsistit, erravitne via, seu lassa resedit, / incertum.
Then trembling seized me and, amidst my fear, / what power I know not, but some power unkind / confused my wandering wits, and robbed me of my mind. / For while, the byways following, I left / the beaten track, ah! woe and well away! / my wife Creusa lost me – whether reft / by Fate, or faint or wandering astray, / I know not.
